analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that stop workers from taking a new job.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to void noncompete agreements — which its findings say cover 1 in 5 U.S. workers — died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to enter into, enforce, or threaten noncompete agreements with their workers, voiding any such agreements. Workers could sue violators for damages and attorney's fees, the Labor Department could fine violators up to $5,000 a week (paid to the affected worker), and the FTC could treat violations as deceptive practices. Noncompetes tied to selling a business or a partnership stake, and one-year noncompetes for top executives with severance, would remain allowed, and trade secret and nondisclosure protections would be untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by noncompete agreements, which the bill's own findings say reach about 1 in 5 U.S. workers across sectors and income brackets. They would be free to change jobs, work for a competitor, or start a business without legal threat, and would gain tools to fight back: a private right to sue for actual damages plus attorney's fees, Labor Department investigations with civil fines of up to $5,000 per week paid to the aggrieved worker, and FTC enforcement. The bill's findings state that noncompetes reduce wages, restrict mobility, and slow innovation [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Voids noncompete agreements for workers engaged in commerce, making it illegal to enter into, enforce, or even threaten to enforce one — covering the estimated 1 in 5 workers the bill says are bound by such agreements.

Gives workers real remedies: any aggrieved individual can sue in federal court for actual damages plus attorney's fees, and the Labor Department can impose a civil fine of up to $5,000 for each week of violation, with the fine paid to the affected worker.
Adds the Federal Trade Commission as an enforcer, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and requires employers to post notices of workers' new rights on the premises.

Keeps employers' narrower tools intact — trade secrets, intellectual property, and nondisclosure agreements — so companies can still protect confidential information without blocking a worker's next job.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use noncompete agreements to keep workers from leaving would lose that tool and would have to compete for labor through pay and working conditions instead, or rely on trade secrets and nondisclosure agreements. Violating employers would face FTC enforcement, Labor Department actions, weekly fines of up to $5,000 paid to the worker, and private lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees. Taxpayers would fund modest new Labor Department and FTC enforcement and reporting duties [S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban does not apply to everyone: noncompetes remain legal when someone sells a business or ownership stake, in partnership dissolutions, and — capped at one year — for senior executives in the top 10 percent of pay who receive severance. The highest earners would keep restrictions that ordinary workers lose.

Employers lose a tool they use to protect investments in training and client relationships. The bill's own findings acknowledge employers use noncompetes to protect their interests, though it argues trade secrets and nondisclosure agreements are narrower alternatives that don't harm workers' job prospects.

Enforcement is split between two agencies — the FTC and the Labor Department — which would have to develop shared standards and divide responsibility within 90 days of enactment, a structure that could produce overlapping or inconsistent enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for workers are large and direct: freedom to change jobs, likely wage growth, and enforceable remedies paid out of violators' pockets. The main costs fall on employers that relied on noncompetes as a cheap retention device, and they keep trade secret, IP, and nondisclosure protections as alternatives. The biggest design weakness is the carve-out for business sellers and highly paid senior executives, which preserves the very practice for the top of the pay scale that the bill bans for everyone else — a two-tier system. On balance, the benefits to ordinary workers clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate's labor committee for the rest of the Congress — no committee vote, no floor vote — and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Todd Young, a Republican, introduced the bill on October 16, 2019, together with Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee held a hearing on the bill on November 14, 2019 (printed as S.Hrg. 116-233), but the HELP Committee, which had jurisdiction, took no action.
No further action was ever taken — no committee vote, no floor vote, no House action — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on noncompete agreements are better off, because they kept the ability to restrict where their workers can work next — a tool the bill said suppresses wages and mobility. Workers covered by noncompetes gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican lead sponsor and a Democratic co-sponsor launched it together, and it never reached a vote, so there is no recorded party split — only bipartisan sponsorship followed by committee inaction.

industries.industry: Employers that use noncompete agreements (tech firms, hospital systems, staffing agencies, service and retail chains)
industries.note: The bill strips their ability to bar departing employees from working for competitors or starting rivals, which the bill's findings say suppresses wages and mobility for the 1 in 5 workers covered. They would retain trade secret, IP, and nondisclosure tools as narrower alternatives.

industries.industry: Business sellers, corporate acquirers, and top senior executives
industries.note: The bill explicitly preserves noncompetes in business sales, partnership dissolutions, and one-year deals for acquired executives in the top 10 percent of pay with severance — so dealmakers and the highest earners keep a restriction ordinary workers lose.
Employers' noncompete drafting work would shrink, but new private lawsuits, Labor Department fines, and FTC enforcement actions would create a different stream of litigation and compliance work.
